description: I am building Mexico Fire Record for the challenge Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. It is a bilingual website that puts NASA satellite heat detections over Mexico from 2000 to 2026 on one scale and shows how much to trust each number. My interests are open data, data visualization and tools that help people act on what satellites see. The project is already built and I am submitting it on my own, so I am not looking for new members.
summary: Mexico Fire Record is a bilingual website that puts MODIS and VIIRS satellite heat detections over Mexico on a single VIIRS S-NPP scale, month by month from November 2000 to October 2026, for Mexico and each of its 32 states. It answers the challenge by rescaling MODIS counts with a monthly factor per state and by measuring the error of that estimate in held-out years, which is 19.5% for a typical state and 5.5% for Mexico as a whole, and it offers an activity calendar, anomalies and a CSV download. It also compares the last 24 hours of detections with that record and lets a person who sees smoke check nearby detections from their phone. It matters because civil protection staff, journalists, fire crews and schools can compare any month with the whole record and also know how far to trust the number.
details:
Mexico Fire Record is a static website in Spanish and English that turns NASA satellite heat detections over Mexico into one consistent monthly record of 312 months, from November 2000 to October 2026, for Mexico and each of its 32 states, and it also shows the health of that record, such as Terra and Aqua orbital drift since 2022 and the 2023 MODIS version change.

The unit is the cell day, a 0.05° cell (about 5 km) with at least one detection on a day. MODIS has 1 km pixels and VIIRS has 375 m pixels, so their counts differ. From February 2012 the series is the VIIRS S-NPP count, and before that it is MODIS (Terra or Aqua from July 2002, Terra alone before) rescaled with a factor for each state and calendar month estimated from 2012 to 2021. In leave one year out validation over 2012 to 2021, the median monthly error is 19.5% across states and 5.5% for Mexico as a whole, since state errors partly cancel out.

Beyond the challenge, Today compares the last 24 hours of VIIRS NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 near real time detections with the S-NPP history for that date, adds the MODIS near-real time count, shows the latest GOES-18 and GOES-19 heat without counting it, draws local NOAA HMS smoke plumes and estimates the next VIIRS swath. "I saw a fire" takes the phone location, a photo's GPS tag read in the browser or a map point, then lists heat detections within 5 km, smoke over the point and the nearest town, and offers "Call 911" and a message to copy or share, and the location stays on the device unless shared. The calendar also writes a citable summary for any month and region and asks whether the fire season moved, and in all 33 regions the answer is no clear shift.

It is built for civil protection offices, journalists, fire crews and schools, which need to know whether a month is unusual and how sure that is, so the site puts the number, its uncertainty and a CSV download together.

The site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework, plus satellite.js for orbits, and the pipeline is Python with DuckDB, pandas, NumPy and PyArrow. A Vercel cron triggers a GitHub Actions workflow that rebuilds the near-real-time snapshot and publishes it only if checks against raw data pass, and 133 automated JavaScript tests cover the site.

Limits we state up front. Validation covers 2012 to 2021 only, so applying it before 2012 is an extrapolation. A heat detection is not a fire verified on the ground or burned area, and no detection does not mean no fire. Each month's band is illustrative, not a confidence interval. August to October 2026 are provisional near real time S-NPP data, and S-NPP delivered no data over Mexico on 15 days in 2026, which the calendar flags. GOES only shows recent heat and is never counted.

Future work: GOES GLM lightning, a fire danger index, Sentinel-3 and TEMPO, with no dates set.
